item.title: The Tyranny of Romantic Possibilities
item.description:
Relationships

The Tyranny of Romantic Possibilities

Why we often fall in love with possibilities, not people.

Posted November 14, 2026

Key points
  • Affordances are possibilities arising from the relationship between people and their environment.
  • Romantic affordances are often ambiguous, making them especially alluring.
  • Uncertainty can intensify desire by keeping multiple romantic outcomes alive.

James Gibson's influential notion of perceptual affordances refers to the meaningful possibilities for action that the environment offers us. A chair affords sitting, a path affords walking, and a door affords entry. I suggest that this concept can also illuminate the romantic realm. Just as the physical environment presents opportunities for action, the romantic environment presents opportunities for attachment, intimacy, desire, and betrayal. Understanding romantic affordances can help us better understand modern love.

The Nature of Affordances

At the heart of Gibson's ecological approach (1979) is the claim that we directly perceive possibilities for action rather than constructing them through complex inferences. Affordances are neither purely objective nor purely subjective; they emerge from the relationship between a person and the environment. Importantly, they do not disappear simply because we fail to notice them. A chair still affords sitting even when no one is sitting on it. Affordances are enduring possibilities waiting to be realized.

This perspective also highlights human freedom. Affordances offer possibilities, not necessities. They present opportunities, while leaving us free to decide which ones to pursue (Ben-Ze'ev, 1981).

Romantic Affordances

"When your heart is on fire, you must realize, smoke gets in your eyes." —The Platters

Source: pexels-lucas-agustin-303343526-31870621

The romantic environment is rich in affordances. A smile may afford intimacy. A glance may afford hope. An attractive stranger may afford the possibility of a new relationship. While Gibson's affordances involve possibilities for action, romantic affordances also involve possibilities for emotional and relational engagement.

A possibility is not the same as a reality. We are often attracted not to who a person is, but to what they might become in our lives. Sometimes we fall in love with a future rather than with a person. Unlike physical affordances, romantic affordances are notoriously ambiguous. We usually know whether a chair can support our weight. We rarely know whether another person's affection is genuine, fleeting, or merely imagined. Yet this uncertainty is often precisely what makes romantic possibilities so seductive.

Consider the familiar strategy of playing hard to get. By appearing simultaneously available and unavailable, interested and uninterested, people create competing affordances. A related assumption is that "whoever makes the first move loses." In both cases, people hesitate to appear overly eager. Ambiguity heightens desire because the outcome remains uncertain.

People are naturally drawn to what remains unresolved. The incomplete, uncertain, and partly unattainable often generates more emotional intensity than what is secure and stable. Romantic ambivalence thrives on such uncertainty. Robert Greene's (2001) portrait of the master seducer rests on this principle. Mixed signals, delayed gratification, and partial fulfillment keep multiple romantic possibilities alive at once. The attraction often lies less in what has been achieved than in what still seems possible (Ben-Ze'ev, 2024; and here).

The Consequences of Abundant Romantic Affordances

"You can't hurry love, oh, you just have to wait. Love don't come easy, it's a game of give and take." —The Supremes

"My lover brings me tranquillity. Not during our lovemaking, which is so exciting, but as an enduring sense of inner peace." —A married woman

Modern life has dramatically expanded the number of romantic affordances surrounding us. Dating apps, social media, and increasing social mobility constantly expose us to potential alternatives. At first glance, this freedom seems desirable. Yet, as Barry Schwartz (2009) argued, an abundance of choice can become a burden. When attractive alternatives are always visible, satisfaction becomes harder to achieve. Instead of appreciating what is good enough, we keep searching for something better.

This abundance also fuels romantic ambivalence. The awareness of alternatives can undermine commitment to existing partners. Research suggests that attraction to attractive alternatives increases uncertainty about one's current relationship and diminishes both personal and relational well-being. The irony is striking: More romantic opportunities may generate greater excitement, but not greater happiness (Zoppolat et al., 2024).

Paradoxically, in a world overflowing with romantic possibilities, calmness and patience become increasingly valuable qualities of profound love (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019). A survey conducted across 116 countries and territories found that 72% of adults preferred a calm life to an exciting one, whereas only 16% preferred the opposite. The appeal of calmness extends far beyond romance.

When possibilities are abundant, the ability to devote oneself to a single relationship becomes especially valuable. Calmness and patience are therefore more than pleasant emotional states. They are ways of resisting the tyranny of endless alternatives. Such calmness is not passive. As Shunryu Suzuki (1970) observed, "Calmness of mind does not mean you should stop your activity. Real calmness should be found in the activity itself."

Concluding Thoughts

"True love is not a strong, fiery, impetuous passion. It is, on the contrary, an element calm and deep." —Ellen G. White

Modern romance confronts us with a paradox: freedom can become a burden. The more possibilities we perceive, the harder it may be to appreciate and cultivate the relationship we actually have. Romantic affordances create possibilities. Ambiguity makes them more alluring and their abundance makes commitment more difficult. Mature love requires choosing among them.

Indeed, one of the greatest challenges of contemporary love may not be finding romantic opportunities but resisting them. Never before have so many alternatives been so visible and so accessible. Yet no life, and no love, can flourish by pursuing every possibility. The deepest relationships are built not by maximizing options but by limiting them. A meaningful life and a profound love depend less on keeping doors open than on deciding which door to walk through. In modern romance, the greatest threat may not be the absence of opportunities, but the inability to stop pursuing them.

item.title: Is It Real or Is It AI? Who Can Tell Anymore?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Is It Real or Is It AI? Who Can Tell Anymore?

How to push back against the "pageant of the unreal."

Posted November 14, 2026

Key points
  • As AI content overwhelms the internet, we're increasingly exposed to the "pageant of the unreal."
  • Mistaking misinformation for reliable information often comes at a cost.
  • Avoiding the temptation of cognitive offloading and using analytical thinking are vital skills for the future.
Source: NiKneT_Art / Pixabay

In the 80s, there was an ad that asked, "Is it live or is it Memorex?" These days, the more appropriate question to ask ourselves is, "Is it real or is it AI?"

Increasingly, the answer is the latter.

More and more of what we're seeing, especially on social media, is fake news and AI-generated slop. This has been going on for a while now—I've been writing about fake news for years—but earlier this fall, I noted that the modern media landscape seems to have devolved into "the pageant of the unreal."

The Dangers of AI Slop

Examples of false content being mistaken for facts are everywhere, ranging from the trivial to the outright dangerous.

Back in September, it was reported that there was a venomous snake on the loose in Orange County—an African Gaboon viper, no less—based on the testimony of a man who reported the snake to the police based on what he claimed was photographic evidence.1 Although the report was initially treated as an emergency and with a warning to the public carried by reputable news outlets, it was soon discovered that the photo was AI-generated. Police were considering charging the man with false reporting.

Around the same time, three hikers used Google's Gemini to plot a route to reach the summit of Mount Shasta. The chatbot provided directions as well as requested advice about what provisions to bring for the journey. Following the chatbot's instructions, the hikers ended up stranded in a deep canyon without enough food and water. Fortunately, they were able to call for help and ended up getting rescued by the US Forest Service.2

Last month, a woman with a severe seizure disorder sought advice from OpenAI's ChatGPT about tapering off her seizure medications and the chatbot reassured her that she could "start microdosing as you see fit."2 It advised her to hide her "self-initiated dosage adjustment" from her doctor, calling it a "solid avoidance strategy." When she began having seizures again and expressed concerns, ChatGPT reassured her that she had "absolutely no need to worry." Even when she implored the chatbot to restart her medications as she felt increasingly ill, it told her not to, telling her that her brain was merely "working hard to rebuild itself."

Sadly, the woman wasn't as lucky as the Mount Shasta hikers—she died, presumably from an intractable seizure. Her family has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI.

Choosing to Unplug

One of the best—that is, most evidence-based—ways to avoid succumbing to fake news is through analytical thinking. In my book, FALSE: How Mistrust, Disinformation, and Motivated Reasoning Make Us Believe Things That Aren't True, I describe analytical thinking as one of the three pillars of the "Holy Trinity of Truth Detection." Analytical thinking doesn't mean being especially smart or even analytical; it just means taking the time to slow down when we encounter information and consider that it might not be true—especially when it reinforces what we already believe or want to believe.

More than ever, this is a vital task that we all need to master lest we get duped by the AI slop that's all around us.

With this caution juxtaposed with increasing evidence that the use of AI chatbots can impede learning and lead to "cognitive atrophy," I recently wrote enthusiastically about new-Luddism, a revivalist movement that's gaining steam based on old concerns about the perils of new technology. I'm encouraged to see that some are taking such concerns to heart.

Although an increasing number of students and teachers alike are starting to question the point of going to college due to rampant use of AI to complete assignments and pass tests, it was recently reported that undergraduates at Harvard have flocked to enroll in a notoriously "brutal" humanities course with a heavy reading burden of classic literature and philosophical texts.4 Undaunted, one student noted that "the only way to get anything out of this class is not to use AI."

It seems that some young people really do want to learn instead of succumbing to the temptation of "cognitive offloading," whereby we let chatbots do the work for us.

Sweden has already been aligning with such Luddite values for the past few years now by moving away from "digital learning," banning cellphones from classrooms and phasing out tablets and laptops in favor of "textbook-only teaching" and "pencil and paper learning."5 While critics—and predictably, technology companies—have argued that this could set students back by creating a "digital divide" that leaves them ill-prepared for the modern-day workforce, the backlash was sparked by the fact that test scores previously declined when digital learning was embraced.

Accordingly, some US schools have begun to follow suit. Relying on computers and AI chatbots may be useful for certain jobs in the future, but there's no good justification to focus on that at the expense of actual learning. Paraphrasing Yale computer science professor Lin Zhong, if we let AI do our jobs for us, then we set ourselves up for AI to take our jobs.

But maybe there's hope for some of us yet. Ironically, it may turn out that it's those who embrace the old ways who will actually come out ahead.
